This is an excellent app, but a species search feature and a report incorrect identification feature would be very useful.

Fun but frustrating. I have learned about many species, especially plants, with this app. It’s accurate and useful… except when it’s not. Every once in a while it’s wildly inaccurate, such as when it misidentified a 15-foot dogwood as 1-foot tropical houseplant. Other quirks are that it frequently locks up after I take a photo so the species doesn’t get recorded in my life list unless I close the app and try again, and there is no clear way to tell it its identification was wrong. I’ll keep using it because it’s more useful than not, but I’m looking forward to future improvements.

Does not give danger awareness!!. My kids love this app and constantly ask me to pull it out to find out what plant or insect they’re looking at. It’s been such a great tool for homeschooling and just plain curiosity! ***BUT my major complaint is it never tells you if something is dangerous, toxic, or any kind of “DO NOT TOUCH” or “DO NOT APPROACH” kind of warnings… it doesn’t even give you the full information on each species, just the very beginning of a wiki page. There are many finicky glitches, but if this app gave the most important information immediately about hazardous species, I would give this app 5 stars! Countless times I’ve had to patiently work through the seek app to identify the species, then I have to open up my browser and type in the name and ask whether it’s toxic/harmful, and then finally get my answer. Sometimes I found out too late because of this long process, and my kid had already grabbed a toxic burr, or a poisonous spider got away in the house, or a highly toxic beetle already hid in the garden, etc. There could be far worse situations with other animals/insects/plants if the app doesn’t add this feature. 
It’s a huge frustration, but I still use it because I can at least identify (hopefully accurately) the species, then make sure everyone is safe before researching it. Just so so wish it could be as fast as a camera click in finding out whether it’s hazardous. Please add this!!

The Best Identification App Hands Down. At this point, iNaturalist is almost unilaterally known by all nature enthusiasts. Seek is a no-nonsense extension of iNaturalist that omits the “social” aspect of iNat. and is pure business in identification. Simply hold the camera over your plant and or animal as it goes through the phylogeny of what it believes you’re looking at until BAM species identified. Once it’s identified you can view a short synopsis of the species and either upload it to your iNat. account or go to a wiki page for more information of the species. If it doesn’t know the species it will at least point you in the correct taxonomical direction of its genus, family, order, etc. And although this isn’t groundbreaking anymore, my favorite feature is that it works offline as well. It also eliminated species that didn’t make any sense geographically e.g. it didn’t try to identify a plant in the Midwest US as something that only grows in Madagascar. Recently, however, the app has been proudly proclaiming that it is using a new model. I’m not sure what that entails, but the app is now 1) slower 2) frequently gets stuck on “Dicot” and 3) has identified several species incorrectly when it gives a species at all. Utterly addicting, but not perfect. This app is often pretty helpful at identifying plants and animals, and is similar to Pokémon Go, except that it’s actually practical and teaches you stuff.

That being said, there are a few issues. I’ve noticed that sometimes the app has a very hard time identifying particular species, including pine trees, bears, and crows, and is very ineffective at identifying deep sea creatures. Often it will misidentify things (leading to some pretty hilarious misidentifications, such as confusing a pheasant for a siamese fighting fish, a cougar for a dromedary camel, a clouded leopard for a leopard shark, and a kodiak bear for a domestic dog). Other times however, it can be pretty good at identifying some rather obscure organisms as well, so plusses and minuses.

Currently my biggest issue with the app though (which is what prompted me to write this review) is the recent update. Before, it seemed as if it was easier to identify things through saved photographs than it was at identifying photos actually taken by the app’s camera. However, with one of the recent updates, the identifying previously saved photos on your device feature seems to have taken a serious downgrade, and now actually seems to do an even worse job than the actual in app seek camera. Could you guys at iNaturalist please fix this issue? Also, could you allow SeekApp to recognize and better identify certain plants and animals, particularly domestic pigs and deep sea creatures (I’m surprised the app doesn’t know what a pig is!)? Significant Drop in Image Recognition Performance for Plant Species. I've been a dedicated user of the SEEK application for the past couple of years, primarily utilizing it for its plant species recognition features. When I first started using SEEK, I was thoroughly impressed by its accuracy and efficiency in identifying various plant species. It was a tool that felt both innovative and reliable, enhancing my outdoor experiences and contributing greatly to my botanical education.

However, over the last year, I've noticed a substantial degradation in the application's ability to correctly recognize or detect plant species. This decline is particularly evident when comparing its current performance to that of the previous year. Instances of misidentification have become more frequent, and the app now often struggles with plants that it once identified with ease. This issue persists despite ensuring that the images I submit are clear and well-lit, conditions that used to guarantee almost certain identification in the past.

The app's diminished accuracy has not only been a source of frustration but has also undercut its educational value. As someone passionate about learning and conserving plant species, the reliability of such tools is paramount. The setbacks in image recognition capabilities have led me to question the updates or algorithmic changes that might have been implemented, which seemingly have adversely affected the app's core functionality.

I hope this feedback reaches the developers and that they take swift action to address these issues. SEEK once stood as a paragon of nature exploration apps, particularly in the realm of plant identification. It would be a tremendous disservice to its community of users if these problems were left unresolved. The potential of this app is immense, and I sincerely hope it returns to its former glory, leveraging the latest advancements in image recognition technology to provide accurate, dependable identifications for nature enthusiasts.
